title: Infrastructure Engineering Consolidated Playbook: GPU Fleet, Cloud Accounts, IaC, CI/CD and Runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
summary: Consolidated playbook for infrastructure engineering covering GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines, and operational runbooks. Provides ownership, SLOs, concrete runbook steps, and escalation paths for production inference infrastructure.
body:
Overview

This playbook documents Redwood Inference's standard practices for operating the GPU fleet and associated infrastructure: cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines, and runbooks used by oncall and infra engineers. It is intended for engineers responsible for provisioning, scaling, and operating inference capacity (hosted, dedicated, private).

Scope
- GPU fleet capacity planning and autoscaling policy
- Cloud account configuration, VPCs, and cross-account networking
- Terraform/IaC module conventions and usage patterns
- CI/CD job definitions for infra provisioning and runtime artifacts
- Runbooks for common operational tasks and incidents

Ownership and Contacts
- Primary owners: infra/gpu-team (pager: #infra-oncall, Slack: @infra-oncall rotation)
- Secondary owners: infra/networking-team (Slack: #networking-ops), infra/security (for KMS/HSM and IAM changes)
- Pager escalation: PagerDuty schedule "infra-oncall" -> "senior-infra" -> "platform-eng-lead"

Key Services and Repositories
- Services: gpu-provisioner, fleet-scaler, cloud-account-manager, k8s-gpu-operator, metal-bastion
- Terraform repos: terraform-modules (modules/gpu-instance, modules/network/vpc, modules/iam), terraform-live (env-specific stacks)
- CI/CD: circleci/gpu-iac (provisioning), github-actions/gpu-images (AMIs/container images)

SLOs and Operational Targets
- Cluster availability SLO: 99.9% per region for kube-gpu-nodes (measured monthly)
- Provisioner latency SLO: 95th percentile time from scale request to node-ready <= 120s for warm pools, <= 5m for cold starts
- Autoscaler correctness: target <2% over/under provision events across a rolling 7-day window
- Incident MTTR target: priority P1 < 60 minutes to mitigation, P2 < 4 hours to mitigation

Capacity Planning and Autoscaling Policies
1. Forecasting
   - Weekly: sync to product usage signals (token throughput, concurrent inference sessions) and upcoming customer commits for Dedicated capacity.
   - Quarterly: capacity review led by infra/gpu with product and sales for large Reserved Commit requests.
2. Buffering and Warm Pools
   - Maintain warm pool equal to 5-10% of sustained peak per region (configurable per cluster)
   - Cold start policy used only for experimental or very-low-util namespaces
3. Scaling Policies
   - Horizontal pod autoscaler for inference frontends (target CPU 55%, target GPU memory utilization 65%)
   - Fleet-scaler for node-level scale: min_nodes, target_utilization, max_scale_delta (default 30% per 10m window)
4. Cost/Performance Controls
   - Use mixed-instance types (A100, H100, and 8-bit-optimized T4-equivalents) with routing policy by customer tier and latency SLOs
   - Apply quantization profiles via model-serving config to reduce GPU memory footprint before scaling nodes

Cloud Accounts & Networking
- Account model: central control account (platform) + region accounts per cloud provider + customer-dedicated accounts for private deployments
- VPC design: hub-and-spoke with shared services in hub (bastion, monitoring, k8s-proxy) and isolated spoke VPCs for quota isolation
- Networking controls: centralized terraform modules for VPC, subnets, route tables, IGW/NAT, peering, and Transit Gateway attachments
- Security: enforce private subnets for GPUs, restrict inbound to bastion and internal control plane CIDRs, use flow logs to S3 for audit retention

Terraform / IaC Module Guidelines
- Module naming: modules/<domain>/<purpose> (e.g., modules/gpu/instance-pool, modules/network/vpc-spoke)
- Semantic versioning: every module publishes a version tag and CHANGELOG.md; live stacks pin to module versions in terraform-live
- Inputs/Outputs: keep variables small and explicit; prefer maps of simple types over nested complex objects
- State management: remote state in the platform account using encrypted S3 + DynamoDB locks (AWS example). For GCP, use centralized GCS buckets + locks.
- Secrets: never store secrets in tfstate. Use vault-provider or cloud kms wrapped secrets injected at apply time.
- Example usage (terraform-live):
module "gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//modules/gpu/instance-pool?ref=v1.3.2"
  region = "us-west-2"
  instance_types = ["a100-40g","h100-80g"]
  desired_capacity = 40
  warm_pool_size = 4
}

CI/CD and Build Pipelines
- Pipeline separation:
  - IaC pipelines: gated by PR review and require two approvers (terraform-modules & terraform-live have separate rules)
  - Image/Artifact pipelines: rebuild container images on base OS or runtime security updates; semantic tagging with build metadata
  - Infra change promotion: plan -> approve (manual) -> apply. Applies only on a tagged commit to master or via the dedicated deployment job.
- Jobs and checks:
  - terraform-plan job runs in PR and posts plan summary as comment with resource delta and drift warnings
  - terraform-apply runs only after 2 approvals and in the target environment's protected branch with manual gate for prod accounts
  - smoke-test job validates node readiness, kube node labels, and sample inference request (local model) post-apply
- CI credentials and least privilege:
  - Use ephemeral CI credentials minted via short-lived service tokens and constrained IAM role assumption

Runbooks (Top-level)
1. GPU Node Not Ready
   - Symptom: nodes in kube cluster showing NotReady or GPU plugin crashloop
   - Owner: infra/gpu-team oncall
   - Steps:
     1. Check k8s node status: kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep NotReady
     2. Describe failing node: kubectl describe node <node> -> check kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet) and nvidia-container-toolkit logs
     3. If driver crash: sudo systemctl restart nvidia-docker || sudo reboot (for persistent driver faults)
     4. If node corrupted: cordon + drain: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data; trigger replacement via fleet-scaler or recreate instance in cloud console
     5. Post-incident: check scheduling backlog and scale up warm pool if repeated within 24h
2. Provisioning Failure (terraform apply fails)
   - Symptom: terraform apply errors on resource creation (quotas, IAM deny, TGW attach failure)
   - Owner: infra/iac oncall
   - Steps:
     1. Inspect terraform plan and error output; run terraform state list to verify partial state
     2. Check cloud quotas and requests: AWS Service Quotas console or GCP quotas API
     3. If IAM denied: check service principal permissions and cross-account role trust policies
     4. Roll forward vs rollback: if partial resources created and apply cannot be re-run, coordinate with platform lead to remove partial resources with terraform state rm then re-apply
3. Network Partition affecting Control Plane
   - Symptom: Agents cannot reach control-plane services, metrics missing, API flapping
   - Owner: infra/networking-team
   - Steps:
     1. Validate VPC route tables and Transit Gateway attachments
     2. Confirm firewall rules/security groups and NACLs were not changed (recent terraform changes)
     3. If cross-account peering is root cause, re-establish peering via console and update route tables
     4. Reconnect monitoring agent and rehydrate missing metrics from agent buffers when available

Operational Playbook and Runbook Hygiene
- Post-incident actions: file incident in status repo, attach runbook steps used, update runbook to cover any gap discovered, assign owner for follow-up action
- Runbook testing: quarterly game-days to validate the top 5 runbook flows end-to-end (provisioning, node replacement, network partition, warm-pool scaling, and security key rotation)
- Documentation: every major terraform module change must include a short usage example and migration notes in the module README

Checklist: Pre-deploy and Rollout Steps
1. Pre-deploy (non-prod)
   - run terraform fmt && terraform validate && terragrunt plan (if using terragrunt)
   - create PR with plan output and tag reviewers
   - run terraform-plan and smoke-test CI jobs
2. Canaries and production rollout
   - deploy to canary region with 10% traffic routing for 24 hours
   - monitor latency and error rates (latency SLOs: 99th percentile < 300ms for small-chat workloads)
   - if stable, increase to 50% then 100% with automated rollbacks on regressions

Appendix: Useful Commands and Examples
- Check gpu nodes: kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu -o wide
- Trigger fleet-scaler: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLEET_API_TOKEN" https://fleet-scaler.redwood.internal/api/v1/scale -d '{"cluster":"us-west-2","desired":50}'
- Example terraform module call (see earlier snippet)
- Example CI job snippet (GitHub Actions YAML):
name: terraform-plan
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init
      - name: Terraform Plan
        run: terraform plan -var-file=envs/staging.tfvars

If you are oncall and uncertain about next steps, escalate to #infra-oncall or follow the full incident escalation policy in the infra SRE handbook.
